Payload shell: maximum volume under a 5 oz budget

Geometry selection · Mass budgeting · Prototype fabrication

The first prototype had one governing constraint: enclose as much interior volume as possible while staying under five ounces, with adhesive counted against the budget.

A sphere is the ideal answer twice over: the most volume per unit of surface area, and no flat face to take a direct hit on landing. It is also not something you build out of flat sheet. My proposal was a cuboctahedron: close to spherical, buildable from flat panels, and critically, fewer seams than the alternatives.

The seams were the whole argument. Hot glue counted against the five ounces, so every joint was mass that bought no volume. That made seam count and usable volume the same problem. Fewer joints meant more of the budget went into enclosed space instead of adhesive. The faceting is a consequence of that tradeoff, not an aesthetic choice.

The program ran this as a hands-on exercise across all five GCC teams so everyone would work the constraints directly. I was paired with the other mechanical design lead. He favored a dodecahedron, which is the more obvious sphere approximation but carries more edges to bond. He built one and it came in overweight. His own volume, surface area, and mass analysis confirmed why, and we went with the cuboctahedron.

The finished shell came in at 4.6 oz against the five-ounce limit and enclosed 138 golf balls without losing structural integrity, the highest capacity of the five teams.

This shell is a prototype modeling the insulation layer rather than the flight structure.

Flight avionics: system architecture

Systems documentation · Sensor and power architecture

The payload logs the full flight, covering ascent and descent profile, barometric pressure, GPS position, and additional atmospheric sensors, with onboard video.

An RP2040 microcontroller reads seven analog sensor channels through two 16-bit ADCs, with an I²C level translator bridging the voltage domains. GNSS and a RunCam over USB-C hang off the same controller. Power comes from an external battery through separate 5 V and 3.3 V regulators, both heatsinked, with a status LED off the regulation stage.

The architecture came from the program. The diagram is mine. I traced every power and signal path through the board and drew it up so the team had a single reference for how the system actually fits together.

Manufacturing engineering intern
May – August 2026 · Phoenix, AZ

An AS9100-certified aerospace sub-tier supplier of about thirty people. I arrived with three assigned projects and left having also run quality inspection for the back half of the summer. Everything below is written at a level that keeps customer and process information out of it.

Induction brazing nonconformance

Process engineering · Root cause · Fixture design

An induction brazed assembly was falling outside its ±0.004" flatness specification, and the manual torch process being used to correct it was too inconsistent to rely on.

Working the problem with the engineering team, we traced it to the base material. It is non-magnetic, which means induction heating gets no contribution from hysteresis loss. All of it comes from eddy currents alone. That accounted for how unevenly heat was landing across the part.

I contributed to the implementation and design of a steel susceptor that couples to the field and delivers heat locally into the joint, and to the revised setup built around it. The new process replaced manual torch work and brings parts within the flatness specification.

Role
Root cause with engineering team; contributed to susceptor design and implementation

Dimensional inspection and rework

Metrology · GD&T · Nonconformance ownership

Inspection ran short-handed through the middle of the summer with a real backlog building. It wasn't in my job description, but I trained on the equipment and ran it daily on top of my own projects.

Optical metrology on Micro-Vu and Keyence systems plus hand measurement, applied against customer prints under ASME Y14.5: thin-wall avionics housings, brazed aluminum assemblies, coldplate chassis, and brazed beryllium copper.

When I caught a nonconformance I didn't just write it up. I built the rework plan with the engineering department, signed off on the report, and executed the corrective action on the floor myself: manual mill and air press setups, pin and bushing pressing, HELICOIL and gasket installation, finishing.

Tooling and job-box locator

Lean · Inventory systems · Adopted standard

A branch merger delivered an inventory with no locating system behind it. Finding one specific tool could take weeks.

I catalogued every entry and gave it a physical address: row, then level, then shelf, sorted numerically so index order matches shelf order. The front end runs in a browser off the shared network drive, so anyone on the floor can search it without installing anything.

Physical labeling and the index were built to mirror each other exactly, so the system degrades gracefully when a box goes back in the wrong place. I trained the floor on it and served as interim tooling manager as a result.

Documentation cross-reference tool

Knowledge systems · Sole developer

Controlled process specs, technical data sheets, and safety data sheets lived in different systems. Finding one specification meant half an hour of digging, and the person digging was usually the only one who knew where to look.

I built a searchable knowledge base across the controlled document set, then added a compatibility layer on top of it, checking adhesive against substrate, solder against flux, and thinner against paint, reasoning from source specification sheets rather than from memory. I trained the department on it before I left.

It flags conflicts, missing requirements, and items needing an engineer's judgment. It surfaces the requirement; it doesn't make the call. That boundary is why engineering was willing to use it.

Role
Sole designer and builder
Corpus
Paint and adhesive specs, work instructions, SDS, TDS

Engineering department

Video work instruction system

Process documentation · Floor training

Operations lived with the people who ran them. If an operator was out, the operation was out with them. Nothing was written down that someone new could follow.

I built a first-person camera rig that records an operation from the operator's point of view, so footage shows the work from the angle the next person will actually stand at. Raw captures were cut into instructional segments by work center.

The part that mattered was not doing the recording myself. I trained the floor to record their own work, so the library keeps growing without me in it.

Role
Built the process, trained the floor
Method
First-person capture, edited by work center
Handoff
Running independently at internship end
125+operations banked
8+hours of footage recorded

Academic projects

Glendale Community College

Warren truss bridge: 403:1 load-to-weight

SolidWorks · Method of joints · Load to failure

A balsa wood Warren truss designed to carry the most load per unit of its own weight, then tested to destruction.

Member sizing came out of method-of-joints analysis rather than intuition. I modeled the truss in SolidWorks with fully dimensioned drawings and led fabrication using shop tools, so the built structure matched the analyzed one closely enough for the prediction to mean something.

It failed at 403 lb against a bridge weighing under a pound, a 403:1 ratio.

Balsa wood
